get_rmse <- function(dataset, specification, approach) {
	x <- blind50$RMSE[
		blind50$dataset == dataset &
		blind50$specification == specification &
		blind50$approach == approach
	]

	if (length(x) != 1) {
		stop(
			"get_rmse() returned ", length(x),
			" values for: ",
			dataset, " / ", specification, " / ", approach
		)
	}

	x
}

get_imp <- function(dataset, specification, approach) {
	x <- blind50$improvement_vs_conventional[
		blind50$dataset == dataset &
		blind50$specification == specification &
		blind50$approach == approach
	]

	if (length(x) != 1) {
		stop(
			"get_imp() returned ", length(x),
			" values for: ",
			dataset, " / ", specification, " / ", approach
		)
	}

	x
}

get_loco_ci <- function(dataset, specification, approach, column) {
	x <- loco60[
		loco60$dataset == dataset &
		loco60$specification == specification &
		loco60$approach == approach,
		column
	]

	if (length(x) != 1) stop("get_loco_ci() did not return exactly one value")
	x
}

get_var_ci <- function(dataset, component, column) {
	x <- var60[
		var60$dataset == dataset &
		var60$component == component,
		column
	]

	if (length(x) != 1) stop("get_var_ci() did not return exactly one value")
	x
}

get_cal_ci <- function(anchors, column) {
	x <- cal60[cal60$anchors == anchors, column]
	if (length(x) != 1) stop("get_cal_ci() did not return exactly one value")
	x
}

get_wrong_ci <- function(anchors, column) {
	x <- wrong60[wrong60$anchors == anchors, column]
	if (length(x) != 1) stop("get_wrong_ci() did not return exactly one value")
	x
}

# Abstract

Human skin permeability measurements are commonly pooled across studies even though permeability depends not only on molecular properties but also on study-specific experimental conditions. We tested whether this heterogeneity can be modeled as a reusable source-associated component rather than treated solely as noise. Three public human-skin permeability resources were used sequentially rather than pooled: the Cheruvu et al. 2022 dataset for development, HuSkinDB for replication in a separately curated database and held-out-source calibration, and SkinPiX for cross-dataset transfer. Measurement-level mixed-effects models separated molecular, residual compound-specific, literature-source, and residual variation. The molecular component was deliberately simple and prespecified, using molecular weight and logP alone (S1) or a six-descriptor physicochemical specification (S2). In Cheruvu et al., source-associated variation accounted for `r fmt(ch_source,1)`% (95% CI `r fmt(ch_source_ci_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_source_ci_high,1)`%) of modeled random/residual variance; in HuSkinDB it accounted for `r fmt(hu_source,1)`% (`r fmt(hu_source_ci_low,1)`--`r fmt(hu_source_ci_high,1)`%). Source-blind hierarchical prediction did not show a reproducible improvement over conventional aggregation: RMSE improvement was `r fmt(ch_s1_blind_imp,1)`% (95% CI `r fmt(ch_s1_blind_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_s1_blind_high,1)`%) for Cheruvu S1, `r fmt(ch_s2_blind_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(ch_s2_blind_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_s2_blind_high,1)`%) for Cheruvu S2, and `r fmt(hu_s1_blind_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(hu_s1_blind_low,1)`--`r fmt(hu_s1_blind_high,1)`%) in HuSkinDB. In contrast, source-aware hierarchical prediction improved RMSE by `r fmt(ch_s1_known_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(ch_s1_known_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_s1_known_high,1)`%), `r fmt(ch_s2_known_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(ch_s2_known_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_s2_known_high,1)`%), and `r fmt(hu_s1_known_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(hu_s1_known_low,1)`--`r fmt(hu_s1_known_high,1)`%), respectively. When entire HuSkin sources were held out, offsets estimated from shared anchor compounds improved prediction of compounds absent from model fitting; among `r matched_n_sources` matched sources, mean source-level RMSE reduction increased from `r fmt(cal_one_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(cal_one_low,1)`--`r fmt(cal_one_high,1)`%) with `r anchor_min` anchor to `r fmt(cal_five_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(cal_five_low,1)`--`r fmt(cal_five_high,1)`%) with `r anchor_max` anchors. A pairwise double-holdout falsification showed that source-matched calibration consistently outperformed an equivalently estimated offset from another source. Finally, one-anchor calibration reduced mean source-level RMSE by `r fmt(skinpix_one_imp,1)`% across `r skinpix_n_sources` eligible SkinPiX sources containing `r skinpix_n_compounds` HuSkin-unseen compounds, all within the HuSkin-defined chemical applicability domain. These findings support a study-aware QSPR framework in which literature-source heterogeneity is modeled explicitly and can be estimated for a new experimental source using a small number of shared compounds.

**Keywords:** skin permeability; QSPR; mixed-effects model; hierarchical model; source calibration; external transfer; applicability domain; HuSkinDB; SkinPiX

# Introduction

The skin permeability coefficient, $K_p$, is a central parameter in transdermal drug delivery, dermal toxicology, cosmetics, and exposure assessment. Because direct measurement in human skin is expensive, tissue-limited, and experimentally demanding, quantitative structure--property relationship (QSPR) models have long been used to estimate permeability from molecular structure. The classical Potts--Guy model relates permeability primarily to lipophilicity and molecular size [@PottsGuy1992], while later studies have explored broader physicochemical descriptor sets and more flexible statistical or machine-learning methods [@TsakovskaEtAl2017; @ZengEtAl2021].

A major complication is that the published literature does not represent a single experimental system. Human-skin permeability values are generated across laboratories, diffusion-cell configurations, skin sources and anatomical sites, tissue-preparation procedures, donor and receptor media, temperatures, analytical methods, and reporting conventions. Interstudy variation has therefore been recognized for decades. Fujiwara et al. modeled a latent common permeability underlying study-specific measurements [@FujiwaraEtAl2003]. Abraham and Martins standardized literature values for temperature and ionization before fitting linear free-energy relationships [@AbrahamMartins2004]. Samaras et al. showed that experimental and formulation conditions materially influence in-vitro human skin permeation [@SamarasEtAl2012]. More recently, HuSkinDB and SkinPiX have made measurement-level permeability records and protocol metadata available in structured public resources [@StepanovEtAl2020; @ChedikEtAl2024].

Recent predictive studies further narrow the remaining methodological gap. QSPR models have been developed from curated HuSkinDB records [@WatersQuah2022], and newer work has combined HuSkinDB and SkinPiX into larger curated resources for predictive modeling [@AsgarkhanovaEtAl2026]. Oh and Ahn explicitly examined disagreement among repeated permeability measurements, protocol variables, record-level versus compound-level modeling, and mixed-effects formulations [@OhAhn2026]. Consequently, novelty can no longer rest on the general observations that repeated measurements disagree, that experimental conditions matter, or that mixed-effects models can be fitted to permeability data.

The more operational question is whether source-associated heterogeneity can be **estimated for a previously unseen experimental source and then used to improve predictions for new compounds measured by that source**. If measurements can be separated into a transferable molecular component and a source-associated component shared across compounds, then compounds measured both in a reference corpus and on a new platform could serve as calibration anchors. Under this interpretation, study heterogeneity becomes not only a source of uncertainty but also a parameter that can be estimated when deploying a model to a new laboratory, apparatus, or protocol.

We therefore considered the measurement-level model

$$
y_{ijr}
=
\log_{10} K_{p,ijr}
=
f(X_i)
+
\beta^\top Z_{ijr}
+
b_i
+
u_j
+
\epsilon_{ijr},
$$

where $K_{p,ijr}$ is the permeability coefficient, expressed in cm/h, for measurement $r$ of compound $i$ reported by source $j$. Thus, $y_{ijr}$ is the corresponding $\log_{10}K_p$ endpoint. The index $r$ distinguishes repeated measurements of the same compound within the same literature source. $f(X_i)$ is the systematic molecular component, $Z_{ijr}$ contains measurement-level experimental covariates, $b_i$ is residual compound-specific variation not explained by $f(X_i)$, $u_j$ is a source-associated random intercept, and $\epsilon_{ijr}$ is measurement-level residual error. For a previously measured compound, the total chemical contribution is $f(X_i)+b_i$; for a genuinely unseen compound, only $f(X_i)$ is available in expectation.

The analysis was designed as development, replication in a separately curated database, and cross-dataset transfer. The Cheruvu et al. dataset [@CheruvuEtAl2022] was used to establish the variance structure and compare conventional compound aggregation with measurement-level hierarchical prediction. HuSkinDB was then used to replicate the hierarchy and to simulate deployment by holding out entire literature sources. Finally, SkinPiX was kept separate as an external transfer set: the molecular model was trained on HuSkinDB only, shared HuSkin--SkinPiX compounds were used as anchors, and SkinPiX-only compounds were reserved for evaluation. The central hypotheses were that (i) permeability measurements contain a reproducible source-associated component not captured by molecular descriptors alone, and (ii) this component can be estimated from a small number of shared compounds to improve prediction at an unseen source.

# Materials and Methods

## Study design and data sources

Three public human-skin permeability datasets were analyzed sequentially (Table 1). The Cheruvu et al. 2022 compilation was used for model development [@CheruvuEtAl2022] and contained `r ch_n_observations` retained measurements from `r ch_n_compounds` compounds and `r ch_n_sources` literature references. HuSkinDB was used for replication of the hierarchical findings and for internal source-calibration experiments [@StepanovEtAl2020]; the processed dataset contained `r hu_n_observations` measurements from `r hu_n_compounds` compounds and `r hu_n_sources` references. SkinPiX was used only for cross-dataset transfer [@ChedikEtAl2024], with `r sp_n_observations` retained measurements from `r sp_n_compounds` compounds and `r sp_n_sources` references after preprocessing. Dataset-specific exclusions and provenance audits are reported in the supplementary material.

```{r table1, results='asis'}
show1 <- t1
names(show1) <- c(
	"Dataset", "Measurements", "Compounds", "Sources",
	"Repeated compounds", "Multi-source compounds", "Role"
)
knitr::kable(
	show1,
	booktabs = TRUE,
	caption = "Dataset structure and role in the analysis."
)
```

The datasets were deliberately not pooled before validation. Their separation allowed development, database-level replication, and cross-dataset transfer to be evaluated sequentially rather than within a single merged corpus. HuSkinDB was treated as a separately curated replication dataset rather than assumed to be statistically independent of Cheruvu at the underlying literature-source level. For the HuSkinDB-to-SkinPiX transfer analysis, literature-source overlap was assessed explicitly by DOI as described below.

## Harmonization and compound/source identities

Throughout the analysis, the response endpoint was $\log_{10}K_p$, with $K_p$ expressed in cm/h. Dataset-specific permeability values were harmonized to this scale before modeling.

In the Cheruvu dataset, canonical compound identity was based primarily on normalized compound name rather than CAS number because the source table contained at least one CAS collision between chemically distinct entries. Reference identity was taken from the literature-source field. The supplied `logkpl` endpoint was already expressed as log$_{10}$ permeability with $K_p$ in cm/h and was retained on that scale. Experimental temperature values reported in Kelvin were converted to degrees Celsius.

HuSkinDB compound identity was defined using SMILES where available, with normalized compound names used as fallback. Literature sources were identified preferentially by DOI and otherwise by the database reference field. HuSkinDB reports log$_{10}K_p$ with $K_p$ in cm/s; values were converted to the common cm/h scale by adding $\log_{10}(3600)$.

For SkinPiX, compound identity was defined from SMILES with normalized names as fallback. Source identity was based on publication identifier and DOI. Exact equality measurements were retained; censored inequality records were excluded rather than treated as exact $K_p$ values. Cross-database HuSkin--SkinPiX compound overlap was identified first by exact SMILES and then by unambiguous normalized-name matching. All resulting overlap assignments were manually audited. No DOI overlap was identified between the HuSkin and SkinPiX sources used for transfer.

Because HuSkinDB and SkinPiX did not provide identical molecular-descriptor definitions, molecular weight and Crippen logP were recomputed from SMILES using RDKit for **both** databases [@RDKit]. All HuSkin and SkinPiX structures parsed successfully. Descriptor concordance among matched compounds was verified in the transfer audit, supporting compatibility of the recomputed molecular descriptors across databases.

## Hierarchical decomposition in the development dataset

The initial Cheruvu hierarchy was examined using nested linear mixed-effects models fitted with `lme4` [@BatesEtAl2015]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_0 &: y_{ijr}=\alpha+b_i+\epsilon_{ijr},\\
M_1 &: y_{ijr}=\alpha+b_i+u_j+\epsilon_{ijr},\\
M_2 &: y_{ijr}=\alpha+\beta_T T_{ijr}+b_i+u_j+\epsilon_{ijr},\\
M_3 &: y_{ijr}=\alpha+\beta_T T_{ijr}+\beta_H H_{ijr}+b_i+u_j+\epsilon_{ijr},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $T_{ijr}$ is donor/skin-surface temperature and $H_{ijr}$ is skin thickness for measurement $r$ of compound $i$ in source $j$.

Compound and reference were modeled as crossed random intercepts. Maximum-likelihood fits were used to compare fixed-effect specifications; restricted maximum likelihood (REML) fits were used for final parameter and variance-component estimation. For presentation, the compound, source, and residual variance components were expressed as proportions of their sum, $\sigma_b^2 + \sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\epsilon^2$. These percentages therefore describe the partitioning of modeled random/residual variance and do not include variation attributable to fixed effects. Because testing a variance component against zero places the null hypothesis on the parameter boundary, the addition of the reference random effect was interpreted primarily using the large change in information criteria and the estimated variance component rather than relying on a naive chi-square test. Temperature and skin-thickness additions were compared using ordinary likelihood-ratio tests.

## Molecular QSPR specifications

The molecular component $f(X)$ was prespecified rather than selected by stepwise search. Two specifications were evaluated in Cheruvu:

**S1: size--lipophilicity model**

$$
f_{S1}(X_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1 MW_i+\beta_2\log K_{ow,i}.
$$

**S2: extended physicochemical model**

$$
f_{S2}(X_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1 MW_i+\beta_2\log K_{ow,i}+\beta_3 MP_i+\beta_4\log S_{aq,i}+\beta_5 HBD_i+\beta_6 HBA_i.
$$

Descriptors were standardized using compound-level training-set means and standard deviations. The molecular terms were fitted jointly with the selected hierarchical structure rather than estimated from pre-aggregated permeability values. The explanatory contribution of $f(X)$ was summarized as the proportional reduction in compound random-effect variance relative to the hierarchy-only model.

For conventional QSPR comparison, measurements were collapsed to a mean log permeability per compound and molecular descriptors were summarized by their compound median. This provided a conventional compound-level benchmark while keeping the molecular information matched as closely as possible to the hierarchical models.

HuSkinDB replication used S1 only because molecular weight and logP were complete for all records, whereas donor temperature was missing in `r hu_temperature_missing` of `r hu_n_observations` measurements and the broader Cheruvu descriptor panel was not available in directly comparable form. Temperature was therefore evaluated as a secondary complete-case analysis in HuSkinDB rather than as a required term in the primary HuSkin QSPR.

Accordingly, variance decompositions from Cheruvu et al. and HuSkinDB were used to assess replication of a substantial source-associated component, not to compare the absolute magnitude of variance components directly between datasets. The Cheruvu decomposition adjusts for temperature as a fixed effect, whereas the primary HuSkinDB decomposition does not.

## Leave-one-compound-out validation and prediction estimands

Prediction was evaluated using leave-one-compound-out (LOCO) validation. In each fold, all measurements of one compound were removed before model fitting and descriptor standardization. Three estimands were distinguished explicitly:

1. **Conventional aggregate QSPR:** prediction from the compound-level regression.
2. **Hierarchical, source-blind:** prediction from the hierarchical molecular fixed effects with all random effects set to zero for the held-out compound.
3. **Hierarchical, source-aware:** prediction using the molecular fixed effects plus the estimated source random effect when the held-out measurement belonged to a source that remained represented in the training fold. If removal of the held-out compound also removed that source entirely from training, the source effect was unavailable and was set to zero.

This distinction was critical because the source-aware hierarchical predictor could use source-specific information when that source remained represented in the training fold, whereas the conventional aggregate model could not. The source-blind prediction therefore served as a direct test of whether hierarchical estimation itself produced a superior transferable molecular function $f(X)$, whereas the source-aware prediction quantified the additional value of source context available from the training data.

Performance was summarized using RMSE, MAE, predictive $R^2$, and compound-balanced RMSE. Sensitivity analyses in Cheruvu examined exclusion of observations with absolute standardized residuals greater than three, descriptor aggregation by mean rather than median, restriction to multi-reference compounds, and an expanded nonlinear molecular specification. These analyses were secondary and did not alter the prespecified primary specifications. Unless otherwise stated, headline LOCO RMSE was calculated across all held-out measurement records, so compounds contributing multiple retained measurements contributed multiple residuals to the pooled error estimate. Compound-balanced RMSE, in which compounds contributed equally after within-compound aggregation, was reported as a secondary sensitivity metric.

## Chemical applicability domain

Chemical applicability was assessed using descriptors only, separately from experimental-source applicability. For every LOCO fold, descriptor means, standard deviations, covariance matrices, and univariate ranges were estimated **from the training compounds only**. A held-out compound was considered in-domain when (i) its squared Mahalanobis distance was below the 95th percentile of the appropriate chi-square distribution and (ii) every descriptor remained within the corresponding univariate training range. S1 therefore used a two-dimensional domain and S2 a six-dimensional domain.

For the SkinPiX transfer analysis, applicability was defined relative to the complete HuSkin training descriptor space because HuSkinDB was the deployed reference model and SkinPiX was external. No SkinPiX information was used to define the chemical domain.

## Held-out-source calibration in HuSkinDB

To simulate deployment to an unseen experimental source, each HuSkin reference was held out in turn. The model was fitted to all other references. Compounds present both in the held-out source and in the training data were considered candidate **anchor compounds**. Compounds present in the held-out source but absent from all model-fitting data were reserved as genuinely unseen test compounds.

For an anchor compound $i$ measured in held-out source $L$, the residual for measurement $r$ relative to the fitted reference model was

$$
e_{iLr}=y_{iLr}-\hat{\mu}_{iLr},
$$

where $\hat{\mu}_{iLr}$ included the molecular fixed effect and the known compound-specific random effect estimated from the training sources, but no effect for the held-out source. If an anchor compound had multiple measurements within source $L$, its residual contribution was first averaged within compound,
$$
\bar e_{iL}
=
\frac{1}{n_{iL}}
\sum_{r=1}^{n_{iL}} e_{iLr},
$$

where $n_{iL}$ is the number of measurements of compound $i$ in source $L$.

For a selected panel $A_L^{(k)}$ containing $k$ anchor compounds, the raw source offset was then

$$
\bar e_L^{(k)}
=
\frac{1}{k}
\sum_{i\in A_L^{(k)}} \bar e_{iL}.
$$

The estimated source effect was shrunk toward zero using

$$
\hat u_L^{(k)}
=
\frac{k\hat\sigma_u^2}
{\hat\sigma_\epsilon^2+k\hat\sigma_u^2}
\bar e_L^{(k)}.
$$

This shrinkage rule was used as a pragmatic empirical-Bayes approximation in which each anchor compound contributed equally after repeated measurements had been averaged within compound. Thus, $k$ denotes the number of chemically distinct anchor compounds rather than the total number of permeability measurements. The approximation does not explicitly account for differences in precision caused by unequal numbers of repeated measurements among anchors or for uncertainty in the training-derived compound random effects.

Predictions for unseen compounds in the held-out source were then shifted by $\hat u_L$. Anchor-panel sizes from `r anchor_min` to `r anchor_max` compounds were evaluated where available. For each panel size, `r n_anchor_reps` random anchor selections were drawn with a fixed random seed.

Prediction error was first calculated separately within each held-out source. For source $s$ and anchor-selection replicate $q$, RMSE was calculated across the unseen test measurements from that source. For each anchor-panel size, these source-specific RMSE values were averaged across the 100 anchor selections and then across eligible sources, giving equal weight to each experimental source regardless of the number of test measurements it contributed. We refer to this quantity as the mean source-level RMSE. Percentage improvement from calibration was calculated as

$$
100\left(
1-\frac{\overline{\mathrm{RMSE}}_{\mathrm{calibrated}}}
{\overline{\mathrm{RMSE}}_{\mathrm{uncalibrated}}}
\right).
$$

Results were summarized both across all sources eligible for a given panel size and in matched source cohorts supporting the same panel sizes. Because the set of eligible sources changes as the required number of anchors increases, inference about anchor number was based primarily on matched cohorts. The `r matched_n_sources`-source cohort supporting all panel sizes from `r anchor_min` to `r anchor_max` anchors was used for the primary HuSkin anchor-number comparison.

## Falsification by wrong-source calibration

A negative-control analysis tested whether calibration improvement could arise from adding a generic offset rather than information specific to the target experimental source. To make the comparison directly controlled, the falsification experiment used a pairwise double-holdout design.

For each ordered pair consisting of a target source $L$ and a different donor source $D$, both sources were excluded before fitting the reference model. Thus, the matched-source and different-source offsets for a given target--donor pair were estimated against the same molecular coefficients, descriptor standardization, compound random effects, source and residual variance estimates, and empirical-Bayes shrinkage rule.

Target test compounds were defined using the ordinary leave-target-source-out criterion: compounds measured in $L$ that were absent from all other HuSkin sources. This test set was fixed before selecting donor source $D$, so compounds did not become artificially novel merely because the donor source was additionally excluded. Candidate anchors for $L$ and $D$ were then defined relative to the common double-holdout training corpus, and a pair was eligible for anchor-panel size $k$ only when both sources had at least $k$ compounds represented in that training set.

For each eligible target--donor pair and anchor-panel size $k$, `r n_anchor_reps` independently sampled panels of $k$ anchor compounds were drawn from the target source and from the donor source. Repeated measurements of an anchor compound were first averaged within compound as in the primary source-calibration analysis. The corresponding empirical-Bayes offsets were

$$
\hat u_L^{(k)}
=
\frac{k\hat\sigma_u^2}
{\hat\sigma_\epsilon^2+k\hat\sigma_u^2}
\bar e_L^{(k)}
$$

and

$$
\hat u_D^{(k)}
=
\frac{k\hat\sigma_u^2}
{\hat\sigma_\epsilon^2+k\hat\sigma_u^2}
\bar e_D^{(k)}.
$$

The same uncalibrated predictions for the novel test measurements in target source $L$ were then evaluated after adding either the matched offset $\hat u_L^{(k)}$ or the different-source offset $\hat u_D^{(k)}$. RMSE and MAE were averaged across anchor-selection replicates within each target--donor pair.

Because a target source could have multiple eligible donor sources, pair-level results were next averaged across donor sources within each target source. The resulting target-source summaries were then averaged across eligible target sources, giving each target source equal weight regardless of the number of eligible donors or novel test measurements it contributed. Comparisons were made within anchor-panel size because the eligible target-source cohort changed as $k$ increased.

The primary falsification contrast was

$$
\Delta_k
=
\overline{\mathrm{RMSE}}_{\mathrm{different\ source}}
-
\overline{\mathrm{RMSE}}_{\mathrm{matched}},
$$

where positive values indicate that calibration using information from a different source produced greater prediction error than calibration using the target source itself.

## Cross-dataset transfer from HuSkinDB to SkinPiX

The SkinPiX analysis was designed as a stricter cross-dataset transfer test. A hierarchical S1 model was fitted to HuSkinDB using RDKit molecular weight and logP. SkinPiX was not used for model fitting. Within each SkinPiX source, compounds also present in HuSkinDB were candidate anchors, while SkinPiX-only compounds were the test set. A source was eligible when it contained at least one anchor, at least one SkinPiX-only compound, and no DOI overlap with HuSkinDB.

Cross-dataset calibration performance was summarized using the same source-balanced procedure as in the HuSkin held-out-source experiment. RMSE was calculated separately for the SkinPiX-only test measurements within each source and each anchor-selection replicate, averaged across the 100 anchor selections, and then averaged across sources. Thus, each SkinPiX source contributed equally to the reported mean source-level RMSE regardless of its number of test measurements.

The same empirical-Bayes calibration procedure used in the HuSkin internal experiment was then applied to each eligible SkinPiX source. Anchor panels were evaluated where possible with `r n_anchor_reps` random anchor selections. Because only `r skinpix_n_sources` SkinPiX sources simultaneously contained anchors and genuinely novel compounds, the one-anchor result across these sources was treated as the primary external-transfer result. A matched `r skinpix_matched_n_sources`-source subset supporting up to `r skinpix_matched_max_anchor` anchors was used only as a secondary anchor-number sensitivity analysis. Larger anchor panels involved progressively fewer sources and were treated descriptively rather than as evidence of a general dose-response.

For compound-level visualization of the one-anchor experiment, calibrated predictions were averaged across the `r n_anchor_reps` random one-anchor selections for each measurement. This visualization therefore represents expected performance over random selection of one available anchor rather than a single privileged anchor choice.

## Uncertainty estimation

Uncertainty was estimated at the level corresponding to the independent validation unit. For leave-one-compound-out analyses, 95% confidence intervals were obtained by paired cluster bootstrap of held-out compounds. Compounds were sampled with replacement, with all measurements from each selected compound retained together, and RMSE was recalculated from the existing out-of-fold predictions. Within each bootstrap replicate, RMSE was recalculated across the retained measurement records, preserving the measurement-weighted primary LOCO estimand. The same bootstrap sample was used for all prediction approaches within each replicate, preserving the paired comparison. Relative RMSE improvement was calculated against the conventional aggregate QSPR within each bootstrap sample. `r n_boot` bootstrap replicates were used, with percentile intervals defined by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

Uncertainty in variance partitioning was estimated by parametric bootstrap of the final REML mixed-effects models. For each simulated dataset, the model was refitted and the compound, source, and residual variance components were normalized by their sum. Ninety-five percent percentile intervals were calculated from `r n_boot` bootstrap replicates.

For the matched `r matched_n_sources`-source HuSkin calibration analysis, uncertainty in mean source-level RMSE improvement was estimated by nonparametric bootstrap of literature sources. `r matched_n_sources` sources were sampled with replacement in each replicate, with the same sampled source set retained across anchor-panel sizes. Improvement was recalculated using the same ratio of mean calibrated to mean uncalibrated source-level RMSE defined above.

For the pairwise double-holdout falsification analysis, uncertainty was estimated by nonparametric bootstrap of target literature sources within each anchor-panel size. The target-source summaries had already averaged across eligible donor sources, so target sources rather than target--donor pairs were treated as the independent resampling units. Matched-source and different-source calibration were evaluated on the same resampled target sources, and the paired difference in mean source-level RMSE was recalculated in each bootstrap replicate.

Formal confidence intervals were not calculated for the external SkinPiX result because only `r skinpix_n_sources` eligible sources were available. External-transfer heterogeneity was instead summarized using individual source results and the number of sources and compounds showing lower error after calibration.

## Software and reproducibility

All statistical analyses were performed in R. Linear mixed-effects models were fitted with `lme4` [@BatesEtAl2015]. RDKit was used in a separate Python environment to calculate molecular weight and Crippen logP from SMILES [@RDKit]. Analysis scripts were organized sequentially so that data preparation, model fitting, validation, falsification, and manuscript output were separated and reproducible. No results were recalculated in the manuscript-generation scripts.

# Results

## Source-associated heterogeneity replicates across datasets

Adding a literature-source random intercept to the Cheruvu hierarchy reduced AIC from `r fmt(m10$AIC[m10$model == "M0"],2)` to `r fmt(m10$AIC[m10$model == "M1"],2)`. Adding temperature further reduced AIC to `r fmt(m10$AIC[m10$model == "M2"],2)`, whereas adding skin thickness increased AIC slightly to `r fmt(m10$AIC[m10$model == "M3"],2)`. The temperature coefficient was `r fmt(ch_temp,4)` log$_{10}$ units per $^\circ$C ($p=`r fp(ch_temp_p)`$), corresponding to approximately a `r fmt((10^ch_temp - 1) * 100,1)`% multiplicative increase in $K_p$ per degree Celsius. Skin thickness was not supported ($p=`r fp(ch_thickness_p)`$). The M2 model was therefore used as the primary Cheruvu hierarchy.

In the REML variance decomposition, the modeled random/residual variance in Cheruvu et al. was partitioned into compound-associated (`r fmt(ch_compound,1)`%, 95% CI `r fmt(ch_compound_ci_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_compound_ci_high,1)`%), source-associated (`r fmt(ch_source,1)`%, `r fmt(ch_source_ci_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_source_ci_high,1)`%), and residual (`r fmt(ch_residual,1)`%, `r fmt(ch_residual_ci_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_residual_ci_high,1)`%) components (Table 2; Figure 1). HuSkinDB reproduced substantial source-associated variation: compound, source, and residual components accounted for `r fmt(hu_compound,1)`% (`r fmt(hu_compound_ci_low,1)`--`r fmt(hu_compound_ci_high,1)`%), `r fmt(hu_source,1)`% (`r fmt(hu_source_ci_low,1)`--`r fmt(hu_source_ci_high,1)`%), and `r fmt(hu_residual,1)`% (`r fmt(hu_residual_ci_low,1)`--`r fmt(hu_residual_ci_high,1)`%), respectively. Because the Cheruvu model included temperature as a fixed effect whereas the primary HuSkinDB model did not, these percentages should not be interpreted as a direct quantitative comparison between datasets. Rather, the replicated result is that a substantial source-associated component was present in both datasets.

```{r table2, results='asis'}
show2 <- t2[, 1:4, drop = FALSE]

names(show2) <- c(
	"Dataset",
	"Variance component",
	"Estimate (%)",
	"95% CI"
)

knitr::kable(
	show2,
	booktabs = TRUE,
	caption = "Partitioning of modeled random/residual variance. Percentages are normalized over the compound, source, and residual variance components; fixed-effect variation is not included in the denominator. The Cheruvu and HuSkinDB decompositions use different fixed-effect specifications and should therefore be interpreted as replication of substantial source-associated variation in a separately curated database rather than compared directly in magnitude."
)
```

```{r fig1, fig.cap="Variance partitioning in Cheruvu et al. 2022 and HuSkinDB. Bars show the relative contributions of compound, literature source, and residual components to modeled random/residual variance. The Cheruvu decomposition adjusts for temperature, whereas the primary HuSkinDB decomposition does not because temperature was incomplete; the figure therefore demonstrates replication of substantial source-associated variation rather than a direct comparison of component magnitudes between datasets."}
include_fig("Figure_1_variance_decomposition.pdf")
```

## Molecular descriptors explain substantial compound variation, but source context drives most of the predictive gain

In Cheruvu, S1 (molecular weight plus logKow) explained `r fmt(ch_s1_expl,1)`% of the compound random-effect variance. The broader S2 specification explained `r fmt(ch_s2_expl,1)`%, only `r fmt(ch_s2_expl - ch_s1_expl,1)` percentage points more. Thus, most of the explainable compound signal captured by these prespecified models was already present in the simple size--lipophilicity specification. In HuSkinDB, molecular weight plus logP explained `r fmt(rep31$qspr_compound_variance_explained,1)`% of between-compound variance.

LOCO validation separated improvement in the molecular component from improvement due to source context. Relative to conventional aggregation, source-blind hierarchical prediction changed RMSE by `r fmt(ch_s1_blind_imp,1)`% (95% CI `r fmt(ch_s1_blind_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_s1_blind_high,1)`%) for Cheruvu S1, `r fmt(ch_s2_blind_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(ch_s2_blind_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_s2_blind_high,1)`%) for Cheruvu S2, and `r fmt(hu_s1_blind_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(hu_s1_blind_low,1)`--`r fmt(hu_s1_blind_high,1)`%) for HuSkinDB S1. All three intervals included zero, providing no evidence that hierarchical fitting alone consistently improved the transferable molecular predictor.

In contrast, source-aware hierarchical prediction improved RMSE by `r fmt(ch_s1_known_imp,1)`% (95% CI `r fmt(ch_s1_known_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_s1_known_high,1)`%) for Cheruvu S1, `r fmt(ch_s2_known_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(ch_s2_known_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_s2_known_high,1)`%) for Cheruvu S2, and `r fmt(hu_s1_known_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(hu_s1_known_low,1)`--`r fmt(hu_s1_known_high,1)`%) for HuSkinDB S1. The intervals excluded zero in all three analyses, showing that the reproducible predictive benefit arose primarily when source-specific information was available (Table 3; Figure 2).

## Shared compounds calibrate completely held-out HuSkin sources

Holding out entire HuSkin references tested whether source information could be recovered rather than assumed known. Calibration used only compounds shared between the held-out source and the training corpus; evaluation was restricted to compounds from that source that were absent from all model-fitting data.

Calibration improved mean source-level RMSE at every tested anchor-panel size among eligible sources. Because eligibility changed with panel size, the primary anchor-number comparison used the same `r matched_n_sources` references that supported `r anchor_min` through `r anchor_max` anchors. Within this matched cohort, mean source-level RMSE improvement was `r fmt(cal_one_imp,1)`% (95% CI `r fmt(cal_one_low,1)`--`r fmt(cal_one_high,1)`%) with `r anchor_min` anchor and `r fmt(cal_five_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(cal_five_low,1)`--`r fmt(cal_five_high,1)`%) with `r anchor_max` anchors. Point estimates increased monotonically with anchor-panel size, although the overlapping intervals do not support interpreting each incremental increase as statistically distinct.

The cohort-level trend did not imply universal source-level success. At `r anchor_max` anchors, `r n_five_improved` of `r matched_n_sources` matched sources improved, while HUR_48 deteriorated substantially. The median source-specific RMSE improvement at `r anchor_max` anchors was `r fmt(med_five_improvement,1)`%, whereas the reduction in mean source-level RMSE was `r fmt(cal_five_imp,1)`%. These quantities differ because the latter is calculated from the ratio of the mean calibrated and uncalibrated source-level RMSEs, rather than as the arithmetic mean or median of source-specific percentage improvements.

```{r table4a, results='asis'}
show4a <- t4a[, 1:6, drop = FALSE]

names(show4a) <- c(
	"Anchors",
	"Matched sources",
	"RMSE uncalibrated",
	"RMSE calibrated",
	"RMSE improvement (%)",
	"95% CI"
)

knitr::kable(
	show4a,
	booktabs = TRUE,
	caption = "Held-out HuSkin source calibration in the matched-source cohort. Confidence intervals were obtained by bootstrap resampling of literature sources."
)
```

## Wrong-source calibration falsifies a generic-offset explanation

The stricter pairwise double-holdout control reproduced the same qualitative pattern as the primary calibration analysis. For each target--donor pair, both offsets were estimated against the same reference model fitted after excluding both sources, so the molecular model, scaling, variance estimates, shrinkage rule, and target test set were common to the matched- and different-source predictions.

At one anchor, matched-source calibration changed mean source-level RMSE by `r fmt(wrong_k1_matched,1)`%, whereas calibration using an offset from a different source changed RMSE by `r fmt(wrong_k1_wrong,1)`%. At five anchors, the corresponding values were `r fmt(wrong_k5_matched,1)`% and `r fmt(wrong_k5_wrong,1)`%, respectively (Table 5; Figure 4). Because the eligible target-source cohort changed with anchor-panel size, these marginal percentages were interpreted within rather than across panel sizes.

More importantly, the direct paired contrast between different-source and matched-source RMSE was positive at every anchor-panel size. The difference was `r fmt(wrong_k1_diff,3)` log$_{10}$(cm/h) (95% CI `r fmt_ci(wrong_k1_diff_low,wrong_k1_diff_high,3)`) with one anchor and `r fmt(wrong_k5_diff,3)` (`r fmt_ci(wrong_k5_diff_low,wrong_k5_diff_high,3)`) with five anchors, with the intermediate intervals also remaining above zero. Thus, an offset estimated from the target source consistently outperformed an equivalently estimated offset derived from another held-out source.

Because both offsets within each target--donor comparison were estimated against the same double-holdout reference model, this result is not attributable to differences between separately fitted reference models. It instead supports the interpretation that the useful calibration signal is specifically associated with the experimental source containing the target measurements.

## HuSkin-trained calibration transfers to SkinPiX sources

The cross-dataset analysis tested the same mechanism under a stricter separation between model development and deployment. The molecular model was fitted to `r rep31$n_observations` HuSkin measurements from `r rep31$n_compounds` compounds. SkinPiX contained compounds overlapping HuSkinDB and SkinPiX-only compounds as documented in the transfer audit. Of the sources containing HuSkin-overlapping compounds, `r skinpix_n_sources` contained both an available anchor and at least one SkinPiX-only compound suitable for genuinely external evaluation. Across these sources, the test set comprised `r skinpix_n_compounds` unique compounds not present in HuSkinDB.

With one randomly selected anchor compound per source, calibration reduced mean source-level RMSE by `r fmt(skinpix_one_imp,1)`% across the `r skinpix_n_sources` eligible SkinPiX sources. Because RMSE was calculated within source and then averaged across sources, each source contributed equally to this estimate regardless of its number of test measurements. At the source level, `r n_skinpix_sources_improved` of `r skinpix_n_sources` sources improved. At the compound level, `r n_skinpix_comp_improved` of `r nrow(skinpix_comp)` unseen SkinPiX compounds had lower mean absolute error after calibration when predictions were averaged across the 100 one-anchor selections. The source-level RMSE and compound-level absolute-error summaries therefore describe complementary but distinct aspects of transfer performance.

`r skinpix_matched_n_sources` of the `r skinpix_n_sources` eligible SkinPiX sources supported at least `r skinpix_matched_max_anchor` anchors. Restricting the analysis to this matched subset, mean source-level RMSE improvement increased across the supported anchor-panel sizes, from `r fmt(match41$RMSE_improvement_percent[match41$anchors == min(match41$anchors)],1)`% at the smallest panel to `r fmt(match41$RMSE_improvement_percent[match41$anchors == max(match41$anchors)],1)`% at the largest. This small matched subset provides supportive rather than definitive evidence for an anchor-number effect across databases. Estimates based on still larger anchor requirements involved progressively fewer sources and were not emphasized.

All `r skinpix_n_in_domain` external SkinPiX test compounds were inside the HuSkin-defined chemical applicability domain. The transfer result should therefore be interpreted primarily as **experimental-source transfer within HuSkin chemical space**, not as evidence for reliable chemical extrapolation beyond that space.

## Applicability-domain diagnostics

Applicability-domain analysis was used as a deployment qualification rather than as an additional model-selection criterion. Cheruvu and HuSkinDB applicability-domain counts are reported in Supplementary Table S7. All `r skinpix_n_in_domain` SkinPiX compounds used in the external transfer test were in-domain relative to the HuSkin training set. Domain-stratified errors and normalized fold-specific Mahalanobis distances are reported in Supplementary Table S7 and Supplementary Figure S1.

# Discussion

## Source-associated heterogeneity is a reproducible part of permeability data

The central result is not simply that a mixed-effects model fits the literature better. Rather, two separately curated datasets show that a substantial component of measurement variability is associated with literature source, and that this source-associated component carries predictive information across compounds measured within the same source. Source-associated variation represented `r fmt(ch_source,1)`% (95% CI `r fmt(ch_source_ci_low,1)`--`r fmt(ch_source_ci_high,1)`%) of modeled random/residual variance in Cheruvu et al. and `r fmt(hu_source,1)`% (`r fmt(hu_source_ci_low,1)`--`r fmt(hu_source_ci_high,1)`%) in HuSkinDB. Because the two decompositions were not based on identical fixed-effect specifications, their numerical magnitudes should not be compared directly. The important replicated finding is that source-associated variation constituted a substantial component in both datasets.

This result is consistent with decades of evidence that permeability depends on experimental context [@FujiwaraEtAl2003; @AbrahamMartins2004; @SamarasEtAl2012]. The present analysis does not claim that heterogeneity is newly discovered. Its contribution is to show that, under a simple hierarchical model, part of that heterogeneity behaves like a **calibratable source-level quantity** that can be estimated from shared compounds and then transferred to compounds not used in fitting.

## Hierarchical fitting does not automatically create a better universal molecular QSPR

The source-blind analysis narrows the interpretation of the LOCO results. Although the point estimates in Cheruvu suggested lower RMSE under source-blind hierarchical fitting, the corresponding bootstrap intervals included no improvement. HuSkinDB similarly showed no source-blind benefit. In contrast, the larger reductions obtained when source context was available had confidence intervals entirely above zero in both development and replication datasets. The evidence therefore does not support hierarchical fitting as a consistently superior estimator of the universal molecular function $f(X)$; the reproducible predictive gain arises from representing source-specific information.

This is scientifically useful because it argues against framing the method as a universally superior estimator of $f(X)$. The data instead support a two-part prediction problem. Molecular descriptors determine the expected permeability of an unseen compound, while source information shifts that expectation toward the scale of a particular experimental system. The value of the hierarchical formulation is therefore not that it always discovers a better molecular equation, but that it separates molecular prediction from source calibration.

The modest difference between Cheruvu S1 and S2 reinforces this point. Expanding from molecular weight and logKow to the broader S2 descriptor set increased explained compound variance by only `r fmt(ch_s2_expl - ch_s1_expl,1)` percentage points. A more complex descriptor search might improve point prediction, but it would obscure the methodological question addressed here and increase the risk that performance differences were driven by feature selection rather than by the treatment of measurement hierarchy.

## Anchor compounds convert an unseen source from unknown to calibratable

The held-out-source experiment is closest to the intended deployment setting. A new source initially has no estimated random effect, so prediction defaults to the reference scale. Once shared compounds are measured, their residuals relative to the reference model provide information about the new source's systematic displacement. Empirical-Bayes shrinkage prevents a small anchor panel from being interpreted as a perfectly known offset.

The matched `r matched_n_sources`-source HuSkin analysis showed a monotonic point-estimate improvement as anchors increased from `r anchor_min` to `r anchor_max`. Bootstrap intervals remained above zero at every anchor-panel size, including `r fmt(cal_one_imp,1)`% (95% CI `r fmt(cal_one_low,1)`--`r fmt(cal_one_high,1)`%) with `r anchor_min` anchor and `r fmt(cal_five_imp,1)`% (`r fmt(cal_five_low,1)`--`r fmt(cal_five_high,1)`%) with `r anchor_max` anchors. However, the substantial overlap between panel-size intervals means that the monotonic point-estimate trend should not be interpreted as evidence that each additional anchor confers a statistically distinct benefit. HUR_48 also demonstrates that a single source-wide intercept is not universally adequate. Possible explanations include compound-by-protocol interactions, condition changes within a publication, incorrect metadata grouping, formulation effects, or other deviations from the common-offset assumption. That failure case should be treated as part of the method's operating characteristics rather than removed post hoc.

Most importantly, the pairwise double-holdout falsification supports the proposed source-specific mechanism. Within each target--donor comparison, both offsets were estimated against the same reference model, eliminating differences in molecular coefficients, descriptor scaling, variance estimates, or shrinkage as explanations for the contrast. The direct difference between different-source and matched-source RMSE was positive at every anchor-panel size, with all target-source bootstrap confidence intervals remaining above zero.

If calibration improvement arose primarily from arbitrary recentering, regression toward an overall mean, or incompatibility between separately fitted reference models, an offset estimated from another held-out source under the same model should have provided comparable benefit. Instead, prediction was consistently better when the calibration information came from the source containing the target measurements. The information recovered from anchor compounds therefore appears to contain a source-associated component shared across compounds within that source.

## Cross-dataset transfer provides the strongest deployment-oriented evidence

SkinPiX was intentionally withheld from model development. HuSkinDB provided the molecular model, SkinPiX-overlapping compounds supplied anchors, and SkinPiX-only compounds supplied the test set. No DOI overlap was identified between the two source sets used for transfer, and RDKit descriptors were recalculated from structure in both databases to avoid descriptor-definition mismatch.

The resulting one-anchor improvement of `r fmt(skinpix_one_imp,1)`% across `r skinpix_n_sources` SkinPiX sources is therefore qualitatively different from an internal cross-validation gain. It shows that a source-calibration procedure developed and validated inside one database can improve predictions in another curated database. The result should nevertheless be interpreted with the correct level of confidence. Only `r skinpix_n_sources` SkinPiX sources were eligible for true anchor-plus-novel-compound testing, and `r skinpix_n_sources - n_skinpix_sources_improved` did not improve with one-anchor calibration. The external evidence is therefore promising and mechanistically consistent with the HuSkin experiment, but not yet large enough to establish the frequency with which calibration will succeed in arbitrary laboratories or protocols.
Formal confidence intervals were not calculated for this external-transfer estimate because only `r skinpix_n_sources` eligible SkinPiX sources were available; treating the `r skinpix_n_compounds` compounds as external validation units would overstate the effective replication.

The fact that all `r skinpix_n_in_domain` external test compounds were inside the HuSkin chemical domain is both a strength and a limitation. It strengthens the interpretation that the experiment tests **source transfer** rather than confounding source transfer with severe chemical extrapolation. Conversely, it means the present study provides no evidence that source calibration rescues predictions for compounds outside the molecular domain of the reference model. Chemical applicability and experimental-source applicability should therefore remain separate dimensions of deployment confidence.

## Relation to previous work

Previous approaches have addressed permeability heterogeneity through standardization, latent common permeability, explicit experimental covariates, filtering, aggregation, and more recent record-level or mixed-effects analyses [@FujiwaraEtAl2003; @AbrahamMartins2004; @SamarasEtAl2012; @OhAhn2026]. The present framework is complementary rather than contradictory. Instead of attempting to remove all source variation before modeling, it retains measurement-level structure and asks whether the residual source component can be used operationally.

This distinction also separates the current analysis from studies whose primary objective is to maximize predictive performance from merged databases [@AsgarkhanovaEtAl2026; @OhAhn2026]. Pooling HuSkinDB and SkinPiX at the outset could produce a larger training set, but it would eliminate the clean cross-dataset transfer experiment. By preserving SkinPiX as an external source collection, the analysis tests a deployment behavior that would otherwise be difficult to identify.

## Limitations

Several limitations constrain interpretation. First, the random reference effect is **source-associated**, not a causal estimate of laboratory, apparatus, operator, skin donor, or protocol effects individually. A publication-level intercept can absorb all systematic differences correlated with that source. The present results therefore do not justify attributing a fixed percentage of permeability variation causally to apparatus differences.

Second, a common random intercept assumes that a source shifts compounds approximately in parallel. The HUR_48 failure shows that this assumption can be violated. Future models could examine random slopes, protocol interactions, or hierarchical decomposition of source into laboratory, apparatus, tissue preparation, and other metadata where sufficiently complete data exist. Such extensions should be justified by new data rather than added solely to improve retrospective fit.

Third, the empirical-Bayes calibration also uses an equal-anchor approximation after repeated measurements have been averaged within compound. Anchor compounds with different numbers of repeated measurements are therefore not weighted according to their measurement precision, and uncertainty in the training-derived compound effects is not propagated into the shrinkage calculation. A fully uncertainty-weighted formulation could incorporate both replicate-specific measurement precision and uncertainty in the estimated compound effects, but this would require a more elaborate calibration model than the simple deployment-oriented procedure evaluated here.

Fourth, the external SkinPiX validation is limited by source overlap. Although `r skinpix_n_compounds` novel compounds were evaluated, they came from only `r skinpix_n_sources` eligible SkinPiX sources. The number of experimental sources, rather than the number of compound measurements alone, is therefore the main limitation on the generality of the cross-dataset conclusion.

Fifth, the chemical component was intentionally simple. The objective was to isolate the effect of measurement hierarchy and source calibration while holding molecular information relatively fixed, not to establish the highest-performing skin-permeability predictor available. More expressive molecular models could be substituted for $f(X)$, but they would require separate validation and should not be assumed to preserve the same calibration behavior.

Finally, the analyses are retrospective and rely on literature sources. The strongest validation would be prospective: fit and freeze the reference model, measure several chemically diverse anchor compounds on a previously unseen experimental platform, estimate its platform offset, and then predict additional compounds before observing their permeability. Such a study would directly test whether literature-derived source calibration transfers to a real new apparatus rather than another historical database.

## Implications for experimental deployment

The framework suggests a practical deployment strategy. A reference model provides a molecular prediction on a common permeability scale. A new laboratory or platform then measures a small panel of anchor compounds already represented in the reference corpus. Their deviations from the reference expectation estimate a platform-specific offset, after shrinkage for limited anchor information. Predictions for new compounds can then be reported together with two separate applicability statements: whether the compound is chemically inside the reference domain and whether the experimental platform has been calibrated.

This creates four qualitatively different deployment states: (i) chemically in-domain and platform-calibrated, (ii) chemically in-domain but platform-uncalibrated, (iii) chemically out-of-domain but platform-calibrated, and (iv) chemically out-of-domain and platform-uncalibrated. The present study provides the strongest evidence for the first state and does not imply that source calibration compensates for chemical extrapolation.

# Conclusions

Human skin permeability measurements contain substantial and reproducible source-associated variation that is not captured by molecular descriptors alone. Retaining measurement-level hierarchy does not consistently produce a better source-independent molecular QSPR, but it allows source context to be represented explicitly. When source-specific information is available from the reference data, incorporating that context materially improves prediction; when a source is new, shared anchor compounds can instead be used to estimate a source offset.

The calibration effect survived two important tests. It improved prediction of compounds absent from model fitting when entire HuSkin sources were held out, and in a pairwise double-holdout falsification, source-matched calibration consistently outperformed an otherwise equivalent offset estimated from another held-out source. The same calibration framework then transferred from HuSkinDB to SkinPiX measurements, reducing mean source-level error for HuSkin-unseen compounds. These findings support a study-aware QSPR framework in which molecular prediction and experimental-source calibration are treated as distinct but complementary components of permeability prediction.

# Data and code availability

The analysis uses publicly available datasets from Cheruvu et al. 2022, HuSkinDB, and SkinPiX [@CheruvuEtAl2022; @StepanovEtAl2020; @ChedikEtAl2024]. Analysis scripts and processed outputs are maintained in the project repository. The final repository release should include the exact raw-data provenance, software-environment information for RDKit descriptor generation, and all scripts required to regenerate manuscript tables and figures.
